title: The 2.0-day TESS signal near WASP-105 b has the transit duration of the K-dwarf host, not of its bound 0.42-arcsec M-dwarf companion, if the planet orbit is near circular
abstract: A TESS search found a 2.0028-day, about 300 ppm transit signal near the hot Jupiter WASP-105 b (TOI-246). Public speckle images show a star 0.42 arcsec from WASP-105, which TESS cannot resolve. We measured the Gemini Zorro images from 2024: the companion has delta m = 3.15 at 832 nm and 4.50 at 562 nm. Its position changed by 14 mas since the SOAR detection in 2020, while a background star would differ by 195 mas. Thus it is a bound M2.5 dwarf (about 3,475 K, 0.42 solar radii, density 5.3 solar) with 4.5% of the TESS flux. We fitted limb-darkened transit models with nested sampling to 102 transit windows in 9 TESS sectors. The transit of b gives the host density 1.21 +- 0.03 solar. For a circular orbit, the candidate gives 0.86 (0.35-1.25) solar; no posterior sample reaches the companion density, for three detrending windows and in each half of the data. With an eccentricity prior for multi-planet systems, the evidence favours the K dwarf over the M dwarf by ln BF = 8.1 +- 0.2. With a wide eccentricity prior, the M dwarf fits with e = 0.5 and ln BF falls to 1.2. Tidal damping (2-40 Myr) and relativistic suppression of Kozai cycles argue for a low eccentricity. TRICERATOPS with the companion included gives FPP = 0.018 +- 0.001 and NFPP = 0.0006 (likely planet, just above the validation limit). If the host is WASP-105 A, the planet has 1.74 +- 0.10 Earth radii. The signal is still seen only by TESS. A multi-band transit test can decide without an eccentricity assumption: the B-band depth is about 320 ppm on the K dwarf and 62 ppm on the M dwarf.
